preamble: A palatalized dental/alveolar stop [dʲ] can be reanalysed as a true palatal stop [ɟ] when the secondary palatal gesture becomes the primary place of articulation. Czech and Slovak did this with the palatalized ('softened') dentals that arose before front vowels in Late Common Slavic: during the Old Czech depalatalization of the 13th–14th centuries softened consonants either merged with their hard counterparts or became the palatals ď, ť, ň, so Proto-Slavic *d before front vowels now surfaces as palatal ⟨ď⟩ [ɟ], where Russian keeps [dʲ]. Macedonian has the palatal stop ѓ [ɟ] as the reflex of the Proto-Slavic palatalized stop *ď (*meďa > меѓа, *saďa > саѓа), where Ukrainian has ž and Polish dz. Recasens (2020) treats such (alveolo)palatal stops as the typical intermediate stage in the palatalization of dentoalveolars.

examples.note: Cf. Russian дед [dʲet], which keeps the palatalized [dʲ].
Cf. Russian день [dʲenʲ] with palatalized [dʲ], where Slovak has the palatal stop /ɟ/.
Reflex of *ď reconstructed as [dʲ]; Wikipedia's Proto-Slavic article also allows a palatal value [ɟː] for *ď, matching Macedonian. Contrast Bulgarian межда, Serbo-Croatian međa.
